newsitem.title: USA: Exxon, Shell report sharply higher earnings.
newsitem.headline: Exxon, Shell report sharply higher earnings.

text.p: Exxon Corp. and Shell Oil Co. Tuesday reported blockbuster results due to sharply higher prices for crude oil and natural gas.

Exxon, the largest U.S. oil company, said its profits jumped nearly 49 percent to a record $2.49 billion, or $2.00 a share, in the fourth quarter, compared with year-earlier profits of $1.68 billion, or $1.35 a share. Revenues climbed to $37.62 billion from $31.50 billion.
U.S. crude oil prices in 1996 were up more than 20 percent from 1995's levels, while natural gas prices jumped 47 percent.
"Fourth quarter 1996 net income ... was the highest quarterly total in Exxon's history," said Chairman Lee Raymond.

"Relative to 1995's fourth quarter, exploration and production earnings rose on the strength of increased natural gas sales in Europe, lower producing expenses and higher crude oil and natural gas prices," he said.
Exxon said refining and marketing earnings declined despite higher sales worldwide as industry profit margins were generally weaker than in the fourth quarter of 1995.
The chemicals business achieved record fourth-quarter sales, it said. While commodity chemical prices were stronger than in 1995, margins were squeezed as a result of increased feedstock costs.
Exxon's stock rose $1.125 to $103.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Shell Oil, a unit of Royal Dutch Shell Group, said its earnings soared 51 percent to $573 million, compared with earnings of $380 million in the fourth quarter of 1995.
Revenues surged to $8.3 billion from $6.5 billion.
"The primary factors contributing to this substantial increase were higher crude oil and natural gas prices," the Houston-based company said.
Shell said its chemical unit's income was $94 million, a drop of $2 million from a year earlier.
Earnings from oil and gas exploration and production totalled $441 million, an increase of $276 million over 1995.

Ashland Inc., a buyer and refiner of crude oil, was hurt by the jump in oil prices, with its earnings falling to $36 million, or 47 cents a share, in its fiscal first quarter ended on Dec. 31. That was down from year-earlier earnings of $87 million, or $1.29 a share, due primarily to lower results from refining and marketing.
Revenues for the first quarter of its 1997 fiscal year fell to $3.4 billion from $3.1 billion a year earlier.

"Rapidly rising crude oil prices late in the quarter led to an operating loss in December and were a key factor in disappointing results for the quarter," said Ashland Chief Executive Officer Paul W. Chellgren.
Ashland's stock fell 25 cents to $43.625 on the NYSE.
